title: The Shadow of Exploitation in Weber's Class Analysis

fields.title: The Shadow of Exploitation in Weber's Class Analysis
fields.abstractNote: This paper has two basic objectives: first, to understand as precisely as possible the inner structure of Weber’s concept of class and its relationship to the problem of exploitation, and second, to use this interrogation of Weber’s work to defend the importance of the concept of exploitation for sociological theory. To understand the foundations of Weber’s class analysis one must look beyond his most synoptic treatments of class in his well-known chapter in Economy and Society on “Class, Status, and Party ” and see how his concept of class is intimately linked to his investigations of the broad problem of rationalization in modern society. Class, in these terms, is the way economic power is distributed when economic action is organized in an instrumentally-rational manner to the greatest degree. The problem of exploitation – the extraction of labor effort from workers – is treated, in this framework, primarily as a problem of technical efficiency and economic rationality in creating work incentives and effective discipline. This leads to a relatively impoverished conception of the nature of antagonistic interests generated by class relations. If theoretical frameworks are identified by their silences as loudly as by their proclamations, then one of the defining characteristics of class analysis in Weberian tradition is the virtual absence of a systematic concept of exploitation. title: Postcommunist Political Capitalism: A Weberian Interpretation

fields.title: Postcommunist Political Capitalism: A Weberian Interpretation
fields.abstractNote: “Political capitalism” is a term frequently deployed in analyses of the economic systems that emerged in the former Soviet block after the implosion of communist autocracy. This crisp, evocative phrase effectively expresses the shared feeling that the transmogrifications of the formerly “planned economies” did not lead to the desired consolidation of a “normal” capitalism. Many would say that by the mid-2000s several East European countries had reached a state approximating “Western ordinariness.” But even they would agree that, at least during the first dozen years of postcommunist changes, the somewhat mysterious dynamics shaping postcommunist “economic domains” were marred by persisting “anomalies,” enduring “atavisms,” and recurring “distortions” which originated in the realm of “politics.” One cannot in good faith dispute that there was something “political” about the way the idiosyncratic postcommunist economies functioned throughout the 1990s.

title: On the Work of Max Weber

fields.title: On the Work of Max Weber
fields.abstractNote: This chapter is the methodological introduction to Max Weber's great work Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft . It contains the basic and most distinctly rational foundations of all scientific research into social phenomena. This chapter explores the elements which construct social science theory, the manner of their constitution, their systemic orientation and the validity of such construction as well as position of social sciences and of societal structures within totality of universal knowledge. The author defines everything that is given to him by his senses, both external and internal, as sensible ; its ability to be able to be given to him through the senses as sensibility ; its specific given sensible object as phenomenon ; and the symbolised presence of phenomenon, through correct judgement as, existence . He defines the total sum of everything intelligible as the intelligible world and the total sum of empowering judgements as rational world. Keywords: intelligible world; Max Weber's great work; sensible world; social science theory
